name: Gareth Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, unions, AI companies, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead trumpet calls in a theatre pit, record short brass cues for radio and teach four young adults. I have a music master’s and thirty years of section work; the players look at me when a cue lands under a line of dialogue. I like that tight entrance, though the late bus after a double show wears me down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How is home supported by those calls?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, my partner is a pharmacist, and our children are grown. We have a mortgage and three months of bills saved; my theatre and recording rates are typical for a senior player, with some similar music work nearby. I use AI now and then to draft my own travel list, but check every venue and paid call against the contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the pit that a faster travel list helps only when doubling fees for playing two brass instruments and late-finish fees are on the contract. I would ask the manager to sign the call sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our theatre season, four pupils and my partner’s wage cover the mortgage. Three months saved gives us some room for a cancelled recording, though I still check what clears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would keep paid theatre, radio cues and four pupils and request written doubling and late-finish fees. In the plateau’s first year I would get my actual pension estimate, compare it with our mortgage and health before any retirement date, and save a tenth of cleared extra radio fees after bills toward four months of expenses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the present bookings. A trumpet fee is only a fee once the late bus home is paid for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does doubling mean in the pit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I switch between trumpet and flugelhorn in one show, so I prepare and carry both. The extra work should have a signed fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the pension statement end your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have not seen the amount. My partner and I need the actual estimate beside our bills before deciding anything.

I would accept **faster travel lists** only beside a real contract.
think: Our **theatre and pharmacy wages** cover the mortgage.
A **three-month reserve** cushions ordinary cancelled recordings.
A signed **late-finish fee** matters when the last bus costs more.
do: Keep **theatre and pupils** with radio cues with written doubling and late-finish fees.
Request **actual pension estimate**; save tenth of cleared extra radio fees after essentials toward four months.
feel: I feel **calm** about current paid bookings.
S0.quote: A trumpet fee is only a fee once the late bus home is paid for.
fieldNote: His **typical senior rates** and three-month reserve support a calm plateau.
An **actual pension estimate** guides timing; occasional AI travel lists remain checked against contracts.

steps.text: Keep paid theatre, radio cues and four pupils; request written doubling/late-finish fees

Save tenth of cleared extra radio fees after bills toward four months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the radio producer which paid brass cues remain after generated tracks get cheaper. I would say the live pit still needs a trumpet player listening to an actor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Radio cues bring about a fifth of my own income, and I expect some orders to fall. Three months saved gives me time to learn something useful, but it does not replace a producer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would ask for written radio cue rates and a paid engineer lesson on a new AI breath-and-timing checker, which flags misplaced breaths,, beyond my occasional AI travel lists. In disruption’s first year I would test only my own nameless trumpet take after the theatre approves local storage and paid use, compare every breath with the printed score by ear, and stop if timing changes or a file leaves the room; I would keep paid pit and pupils.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about recording fees shrinking. An AI music checker can catch a breath mark; it cannot sign a radio order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a pupil’s recording enter the test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would use my own take without names. Any other player’s file would need written permission and approved storage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the lesson costs you a show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not go. The engineer lesson must be paid outside booked pit hours or I keep the score I already use.

I would defend **live pit listening** alongside generated tracks.
think: I expect **radio orders** worth a fifth of pay to shrink.
Our **three-month reserve** buys time, not a client.
do: Keep **paid pit and pupils**; request written radio rates.
Learn **new timing checker** only in paid lesson outside pit hours with approved local storage and own nameless take.
Compare **each breath** by ear and score; stop altered timing or file leakage.
feel: I feel **anxious** about likely radio-fee losses.
S1.quote: An AI music checker can catch a breath mark; it cannot sign a radio order.
fieldNote: The **new checker** is distinct from his occasional AI travel lists.
Paid **instruction and approved storage** keep rehearsals paid and prevent pupil or colleague audio exposure.

steps.text: Keep paid pit and four pupils; request written radio cue rates
Learn timing checker through paid lesson outside calls using own nameless take and approved local storage
Compare breaths by ear/score; stop timing errors or file leaks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the brass that thinking AGI around 2028 could sell radio cues before robot trumpet players arrive around 2031. I would ask for signed live pit dates now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most radio cues and some paid preparation to disappear in 2028, taking close to a third of my pay. I have lain awake adding the mortgage and bus costs; the live pit may last longer, but I cannot bet on its full calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I would total radio and preparation invoices and keep signed pit and pupil hours. In the first year after 2028, if those fees go, I would seek a posted paid school brass-ensemble lead role only if my music master’s and trumpet leadership meet the requirements, actual in-person teaching and preparation are paid, and written net pay after travel replaces lost fees with a workable last bus; I would keep current music until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about a large expected cut to my own pay. Some schools hire nearby. Only a posted paid opening can replace an invoice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the school pay a person to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would hear a young trumpeter press too hard and adjust the passage in the room. A school must post and pay for those live coaching hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why plan before robot trumpeters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The radio producer can switch in 2028. The card puts hands-on robot players around 2031, three years later.

say: I would separate **2028 thinking AGI** from robot trumpeters around 2031.
I would request **signed pit dates** now.
think: I expect **radio and preparation pay** near a third of income to end.
do: Keep **pit and pupils** with signed hours before 2028.
Seek **posted paid brass lead** after fee loss; require accepted master’s/trumpet leadership and paid in-person teaching/preparation.
Require **written replacement net** after travel and workable bus; keep music until signed offer.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by expected large recording losses.
S2.quote: Only a posted paid opening can replace an invoice.
fieldNote: The **2028 loss** affects radio recordings before robot trumpeters arrive around 2031.
A **school move** needs accepted qualifications, real paid live duties and written replacement net after travel.

steps.text: Keep paid pit and four pupils; total invoices and secure signed dates before 2028
Seek posted paid brass lead after lost fees; require accepted master’s/trumpet leadership and paid coaching/prep
Verify written replacement net after travel and last bus; retain music until signed offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the pit that five years until thinking AGI around 2031 is time to check paid sound work, while robot trumpeters arrive around 2034. I would not call a free course a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Radio cues may fade, and late pit travel is harder on me now. I have carried speakers but never qualified to run the desk; a funded course would be useful only if a venue has a real paid assistant opening for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This spring I would ask a venue about posted paid sound-assistant work and enrol in a live-sound certificate only after it confirms a funded place with paid training hours, a timetable protecting pit and pupil wages, the last bus, and written acceptance of the certificate for its posting before enrolment. In the first year after 2031, if radio or pit fees fall, I would apply after completing the recognised certificate; I would move only on a signed written net offer after travel replacing lost income with a workable bus, keep current music until then, and begin technician-supervised checks without solo crowded shows before signed equipment and safety clearance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the possible fee slide, though five years gives me time to test a paid course. A sound certificate can open a door; it cannot pay this month’s mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you run a crowded desk straight after class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A venue technician would supervise my first checks. I would wait for signed equipment and safety clearance before doing a crowded show alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the funded place pays tuition only?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not enrol. The training hours must be paid and my pit and pupil income must survive the timetable.

I would separate **2031 thinking AGI** from robot trumpeters around 2034.
think: Radio **cues may fade** while pit travel grows tiring.
An **unpaid certificate** cannot replace present wages.
A **posted assistant role** must recognise the completed course.
do: Enrol in **funded sound course** only with paid hours, protected pit/pupil wages, last bus and posting acceptance before enrolment.
Apply **after 2031 loss** to posted paid assistant role with completed accepted certificate.
Move **only on signed offer** with written replacement net after travel/bus; retain music and use supervised checks until safety clearance.
feel: I feel **anxious** about possible fees with a paid option.
S3.quote: A sound certificate can open a door; it cannot pay this month’s mortgage.
fieldNote: The **course gate** protects current pit/pupil wages and requires paid hours, transport and certificate recognition before enrolment.

Keep paid pit and pupils until signed written net offer replaces loss after travel/bus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children that thinking AGI around 2036 and robot trumpeters around 2039 are separate dates. I would still ask the theatre for next season’s paid call sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I might prefer fewer late buses, but I have not seen an actual pension estimate. Our present theatre and pharmacy wages cover bills, though three months saved is not a lifetime income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep pit dates and four pupils, request my actual pension estimate and a signed live renewal, and save a tenth of cleared extra radio fees after mortgage, food and travel toward four months. In the first year after 2036, if recording and preparation fees fall, I would seek a posted paid school brass-ensemble lead role only if my master’s and trumpet leadership qualify, in-person teaching and preparation remain paid, and written net pay after travel replaces the loss with a workable bus; I would keep current music until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about distant radio work while current wages still cover home. I would use a real pension figure before cutting any paid pit call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you assume a pension at 68?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would request the actual estimate and compare it with the mortgage and health. Our calendar has no retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no brass job is posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid pit and pupil dates while they last. A title on a forecast does not pay a trumpet player.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because radio and preparation fees could take a third of my income quickly. Signed pit dates, a real paid brass job accepting my master’s and written net pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the brass player to wait for the last bus after a double show. The pit goes dark long before the journey is over.

headlineQuote: The pit goes dark long before the journey is over.
portrait: Gareth is a **senior trumpet leader** with a music master’s, theatre pit work, radio cues and four pupils.
He has **three months saved**, typical senior rates, a pharmacist partner, grown children and a mortgage.
He uses **AI occasionally** for travel and learns a new checker only with paid instruction and manual listening.
He considers **funded sound training** only with paid time, protected wages, an accepted certificate and supervised first checks.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** could end radio and preparation fees worth near a third of his income.
whatWouldHelp: He needs **signed pit dates**, an actual paid brass post and written replacement net after travel.
